title: Data Modeling Using the Entity–Relationship Model

questions.prompt: In database design, what are functional requirements?
choices: User-defined database operations and transactions required by intended user groups
The entity types, relationships, and constraints describing required data
The DBMS-specific schema produced by translating a conceptual schema
The internal file structures and indexes used to store database files
questions.explanation: Functional requirements describe user-defined database operations, including retrievals and updates; the other choices describe schema or storage design. (§3.1)

image.alt: A data structure diagram next to a data dictionary describing the data elements.

questions.prompt: Which statements describe functional requirements in the database design process? Select all that apply.
choices: A DBMS-specific schema produced when a conceptual model is mapped.
They include user-defined operations to be applied to the database.
They include both retrievals and updates.
Indexes and access paths for physical data storage.
questions.explanation: Functional requirements describe the operations users need, including retrievals and updates. Indexes and DBMS-specific schemas belong to later physical and logical design. (§3.1)

image.alt: A data structure diagram next to a data dictionary describing the data elements.

questions.prompt: Before choosing a DBMS or storage layout, designers need an artifact that describes required data and helps check for missing or conflicting user requirements. Which artifact serves this purpose?
choices: The transaction implementation
The logical schema in a specific DBMS model
The internal schema
The high-level conceptual schema
questions.explanation: The conceptual schema describes users’ data requirements without implementation details and can be used to check coverage and conflicts. (§3.1)

image.alt: A sample entity relationship diagram showing entities, relationships and cardinalities.

questions.prompt: A company database is designed to track employees, departments, projects, and employee dependents for insurance. Which groups belong in its subject area?
choices: Employees, departments, projects, and dependents
Customers, accounts, deposits, and withdrawals
Suppliers, parts, and projects
Students, courses, instructors, and class sections
questions.explanation: The COMPANY miniworld describes employees, departments, projects, and dependents kept for insurance purposes. (§3.2)

image.alt: ER diagram in Chen notation with entity rectangles, attribute ovals and relationship diamonds.

questions.prompt: A company policy permits employees to work on projects controlled by departments other than their own. An employee is assigned to such a project. Is the assignment allowed?
choices: Yes, but only when the employee also manages the controlling department.
No; an employee may work only on projects controlled by the employee’s department.
Yes; employees may work on projects not controlled by their department.
No; each project must be controlled by the employee who works on it.
questions.explanation: The COMPANY requirements explicitly allow an employee to work on projects that are not controlled by the department to which the employee is assigned. (§3.2)

image.alt: Two entity types joined by a relationship in a simple ER diagram.

questions.prompt: An employer needs each DEPENDENT record for insurance to store the dependent’s first name, sex, birth date, and relationship to the employee. Which set of details matches that requirement?
choices: First name, office, phone, rank, and courses taught
First name, sex, birth date, and relationship to the employee
Social Security number, salary, address, and supervisor
Department, manager, locations, and projects
questions.explanation: The stated dependent data includes given name, sex, birth date, and the dependent’s relationship to the employee. (§3.2)

image.alt: An entity box shown together with one of its attributes in an ER diagram.

questions.prompt: What is an entity in the ER model?
choices: A named collection of attributes shared by similar objects
A rule limiting the number of related objects
A value set that can be assigned to an attribute
A real-world object with independent existence
questions.explanation: An entity is a real-world object with an independent existence; it may have physical or conceptual existence. (§3.3)

image.alt: ER diagram in Chen notation with entity rectangles, attribute ovals and relationship diamonds.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly distinguishes the EMPLOYEE entity type from its entity set?
choices: Entity type: shared attributes; entity set: current entities.
The employee key identifies its entity set.
The entity type is a relationship among employees; the entity set is their attributes.
The entity type is the current employees; the entity set is their shared structure.
questions.explanation: An entity type describes the shared structure of entities, while its entity set is the collection of its entities at a particular time. (§3.3)

image.alt: Two entity types joined by a relationship in a simple ER diagram.

questions.prompt: Which statements correctly classify ER attribute examples? Select all that apply.
choices: Birth_date is derived from Age, so Age is the stored attribute.
Address can be composite when users refer to components such as street and city.
College_degrees can be multivalued for a person.
Age can be derived from a stored Birth_date and the current date.
questions.explanation: An address can be composite, college degrees can be multivalued, and age can be derived from a stored birth date. Birth date is stored rather than derived from age (§3.3).

image.alt: An entity box shown together with one of its attributes in an ER diagram.

questions.prompt: When is it useful to model an attribute such as Address as composite?
choices: When users need to refer to meaningful components separately
When every entity must have several values for the attribute
When its value is calculated from another attribute
When it uniquely identifies each entity without using any other attribute
questions.explanation: Composite attributes are useful when users sometimes treat a value as a whole and sometimes refer to meaningful component values. (§3.3)

image.alt: An entity box shown together with one of its attributes in an ER diagram.

questions.prompt: What property must a key attribute have for an entity type?
choices: It must be selected as the primary key in the ER model.
Its value is the same for every entity in the set.
Values uniquely identify entities of that type within the entity set.
It can be omitted whenever its value is unknown.
questions.explanation: A key attribute’s values must distinguish every entity in any entity set of that type; the ER model described here does not designate a primary key. (§3.3)

image.alt: A table annotated with relational terms such as attribute, tuple and key.

questions.prompt: In an ER schema, which situations can a NULL attribute value represent? Select all that apply.
choices: Height is known but its value is missing.
Whether a person has a home phone is unknown.
A duplicate key value that breaks entity uniqueness.
Apartment number is inapplicable to a single-family home.
questions.explanation: NULL can mean not applicable, a value exists but is missing, or it is unknown whether a value exists. It does not represent a violation of a key’s uniqueness constraint. (§3.3)

image.alt: An entity box shown together with one of its attributes in an ER diagram.

questions.prompt: A relational design records `CONTROLS(Department, Project)`, `WORKS_FOR(Employee, Department)`, and `MANAGES(Department, Employee, Start_date)`. Which department value can be calculated by counting related tuples rather than stored as an attribute?
choices: The location of each project it controls
The department’s unique number
The number of employees related to the department
The start date on which its manager began managing
questions.explanation: The number of employees in a department can be calculated by counting its WORKS_FOR tuples. Department number is a stored identifier; project locations and manager start dates are not counts derived from related tuples (§3.3).

image.alt: A table annotated with relational terms such as attribute, tuple and key.

questions.prompt: A CAR is identified by the combination of Registration State and Number. What makes this composite key minimal?
choices: The combination is chosen as a primary key before the ER design is mapped.
Neither component alone uniquely identifies a CAR.
The combination includes every attribute of CAR, so no other key can exist.
Each component has its own unique values, so either is a separate key.
questions.explanation: A composite key is minimal when every component is necessary for uniqueness; neither State nor Registration Number alone identifies a CAR (§3.3).

image.alt: A table annotated with relational terms such as attribute, tuple and key.

questions.prompt: A preliminary ER design has not yet introduced relationship types. EMPLOYEE entities may work on many PROJECT entities, and `Hours` is specific to each employee-project pair. Which representation can store each project together with its hours on EMPLOYEE?
choices: A derived Project_count attribute of DEPARTMENT
A key attribute Hours on PROJECT
A single-valued Hours attribute on EMPLOYEE
Multivalued composite Works_on(Project, Hours)
questions.explanation: The preliminary design uses a multivalued composite Works_on attribute containing Project and Hours; it is later refined into the M:N WORKS_ON relationship. (§3.3)

image.alt: Two entity types joined by a relationship in a simple ER diagram.

questions.prompt: What does an ER relationship type define?
choices: Associations among participating entities of types in the ER schema
A set of allowed values for one simple attribute
A collection of entities that share the same attributes
A storage structure used to connect database files
questions.explanation: A relationship type defines associations among entities drawn from the participating entity types. (§3.4)

image.alt: ER diagram in Chen notation with entity rectangles, attribute ovals and relationship diamonds.

questions.prompt: What does one relationship instance in a relationship among EMPLOYEE and DEPARTMENT associate?
choices: A DEPARTMENT entity and one of its attribute values
One EMPLOYEE entity and one DEPARTMENT entity
Any number of EMPLOYEE entities and no DEPARTMENT entity
One EMPLOYEE entity and all departments in the entity set
questions.explanation: Each relationship instance associates exactly one entity from each participating type; WORKS_FOR therefore links one employee with one department. (§3.4)

image.alt: ER diagram in Chen notation with entity rectangles, attribute ovals and relationship diamonds.

questions.prompt: What is the degree of a binary relationship type?
choices: Each entity can participate in at most two instances.
It has two possible cardinality ratios.
It has two participating entity types.
It has two attributes on each entity type.
questions.explanation: Relationship degree counts participating entity types; a degree-two relationship is binary. (§3.4)

image.alt: An ER diagram in which a relationship diamond carries its own attribute.

questions.prompt: What does total participation of an entity type in a relationship mean?
choices: Every entity of that type must participate in exactly one relationship instance.
The entity type can participate in an unlimited number of instances.
All entity types participate in the relationship.
Every entity participates in at least one instance.
questions.explanation: Total participation requires every entity in the entity set to be related through at least one instance; it does not by itself set a maximum. (§3.4)

image.alt: Two entities related in crow's foot notation, with line-end symbols for optionality and multiplicity.

questions.prompt: Every EMPLOYEE works for at most one DEPARTMENT, while one DEPARTMENT may have many employees. What is the cardinality ratio, written DEPARTMENT:EMPLOYEE, for WORKS_FOR?
choices: 1:N, one department for each employee at most and many employees per department
N:1 (many departments per employee, one employee per department)
M:N (many departments per employee and many employees per department)
1:1 (one department per employee and one employee per department)
questions.explanation: A department can be related to many employees and an employee to at most one department, giving 1:N from DEPARTMENT to EMPLOYEE. (§3.4)

image.alt: The same one-to-many relationship drawn in several ER notations side by side.

questions.prompt: A company rule says that every employee must work for a department. Which participation constraint follows for EMPLOYEE in WORKS_FOR?
choices: A derived participation constraint based on employee count
Partial participation, because some employees may lack a department
Total participation: every employee must be in WORKS_FOR
A 1:1 cardinality ratio, because every employee has a department
questions.explanation: The rule requires every EMPLOYEE entity to participate in WORKS_FOR, which is total participation (existence dependency). (§3.4)

image.alt: Two entities related in crow's foot notation, with line-end symbols for optionality and multiplicity.

questions.prompt: A 1:N relationship has an attribute that records when the association began. If the designer migrates that attribute to an entity type, where can it go without losing the relationship-specific value?
choices: To neither entity type under any circumstances
Only to the entity type on the N-side
Only to the entity type on the 1-side
To either participating entity type with no constraint
questions.explanation: In a 1:N relationship, the attribute can be migrated to the N-side because each N-side entity participates in at most one relationship instance. (§3.4)

image.alt: An ER diagram in which a relationship diamond carries its own attribute.

questions.prompt: In COMPANY, an employee may work on many projects and each project may have many employees. Hours varies by employee-project pair. Where should Hours be modeled?
choices: As a key attribute of DEPARTMENT, since departments control projects
As an attribute of EMPLOYEE, since each employee has one total weekly-hours value
As an attribute of PROJECT, since each project has one hours value for all employees
As an attribute of the M:N WORKS_ON relationship, since the pair determines it
questions.explanation: Hours is determined by the combination of an employee and a project, so it belongs to the M:N WORKS_ON relationship rather than either entity alone. (§3.4)

image.alt: An ER diagram in which a relationship diamond carries its own attribute.

questions.prompt: In recursive SUPERVISION, EMPLOYEE participates once as supervisor and once as supervisee. Each supervisee has at most one direct supervisor, while a supervisor may supervise many employees. What does the relationship design require?
choices: A 1:N supervisor-to-supervisee ratio with role names
M:N ratio, without supervisor or supervisee roles
A 1:1 ratio with a separate supervisor entity
A ternary relationship with three named roles
questions.explanation: The supervisor role relates to many supervisees, while each supervisee has at most one supervisor; role names distinguish the same entity type’s two participations. (§3.4)

image.alt: A UML class diagram where one class has an association with itself.

questions.prompt: What makes an entity type weak in the ER model?
choices: Its entities have values that are unknown when first entered.
No key of its own; identified by owner key and partial key.
It participates in at least one relationship with total participation.
It has only one attribute and no relationship attributes.
questions.explanation: A weak entity type lacks its own key; its entities are identified through an owner entity and a partial key value. (§3.5)

image.alt: An ER diagram that includes a weak entity type with its identifying relationship.

questions.prompt: Two employees may each have a dependent named Alex, and DEPENDENT has no independent key. In COMPANY, what identifies one such dependent?
choices: The department controlling the employee’s current project
The dependent’s Birth_date alone, because dates identify people
The employee owner plus the dependent’s partial key
The dependent’s Name alone, because names are globally unique
questions.explanation: The employee is the owner, and the dependent name can distinguish dependents belonging to that same employee; another employee may have a dependent with the same name. (§3.5)

image.alt: An ER diagram that includes a weak entity type with its identifying relationship.

questions.prompt: A DRIVER_LICENSE cannot exist unless linked to a PERSON, but it has a unique License_number of its own. Is DRIVER_LICENSE weak solely because of this dependency?
choices: Yes; the PERSON entity must be part of every key in the ER model.
No; a driver license cannot participate in a relationship with a person.
Yes; any entity with total participation in a relationship is weak.
No; License_number is its own key.
questions.explanation: An entity can depend on another for existence and still be strong if it has its own key. A DRIVER_LICENSE with a unique License_number is therefore not weak (§3.5).

image.alt: ER notation for regular and weak entity types drawn side by side.

questions.prompt: `DEPARTMENT(Number, Locations, Manager, Manager_start_date)` stores a manager identifier and the date that person began managing it. If `MANAGES(Department, Employee, Start_date)` represents the manager link and its start date, which DEPARTMENT attributes can be removed? Select all that apply.
choices: Manager_start_date (recorded for MANAGES)
Number, a DEPARTMENT identifier
Locations, the multivalued attribute
Manager (represented by MANAGES)
questions.explanation: MANAGES represents both the manager link and its start date, so the matching stored DEPARTMENT attributes are redundant. Number identifies the department, and Locations remains a department property (§3.7).

image.alt: An ER diagram in which a relationship diamond carries its own attribute.

questions.prompt: Users confirm that every DEPARTMENT must have a manager, but not every EMPLOYEE manages a department. What participation constraints follow for MANAGES?
choices: DEPARTMENT total; EMPLOYEE partial in MANAGES
Both EMPLOYEE and DEPARTMENT partial
EMPLOYEE total; DEPARTMENT partial
Both EMPLOYEE and DEPARTMENT total
questions.explanation: Every department must participate in MANAGES, so DEPARTMENT is total; only some employees manage, so EMPLOYEE is partial. (§3.6)

image.alt: Two entities related in crow's foot notation, with line-end symbols for optionality and multiplicity.

questions.prompt: Each PROJECT is controlled by a department, but some DEPARTMENT entities control no projects. What are the participation constraints in CONTROLS?
choices: Both PROJECT and DEPARTMENT partial
PROJECT total; DEPARTMENT partial
PROJECT partial; DEPARTMENT total
Both PROJECT and DEPARTMENT total
questions.explanation: Every project participates in CONTROLS, whereas a department may control none; therefore PROJECT is total and DEPARTMENT is partial. (§3.6)

image.alt: Two entities related in crow's foot notation, with line-end symbols for optionality and multiplicity.

questions.prompt: Which ER notation convention marks a weak entity type, its identifying relationship, and its partial key?
choices: A dotted rectangle, a double oval, and an unmarked partial key
A double oval, a dotted relationship line, and a bold partial key
A double rectangle and double diamond; dotted or dashed partial-key underline
A single rectangle, a single identifying diamond, and a solid partial-key underline
questions.explanation: Weak entities use double rectangles, their identifying relationships use double diamonds, and partial keys have a dotted or dashed underline. (§3.7)

image.alt: An ER diagram that includes a weak entity type with its identifying relationship.

questions.prompt: When mapping a narrative requirements description to an initial ER schema, which wording clue is often useful?
choices: Sentence order determines entity keys, while repeated words determine cardinality.
Nouns often suggest entity types, and verbs often suggest relationship types.
Verbs often suggest key attributes, and adjectives often suggest entity sets.
Nouns always suggest relationship types, and verbs always suggest attributes.
questions.explanation: As a general naming practice, nouns in the requirements tend to give rise to entity types and verbs to relationship types. (§3.7)

image.alt: A sample entity relationship diagram showing entities, relationships and cardinalities.

questions.prompt: A draft schema stores `Department` separately on STUDENT, INSTRUCTOR, and COURSE. Users say departments have names and relationships of their own. Which refinement removes repeated department data and lets departments participate in their own relationships?
choices: Replace the three entity types with one multivalued Department attribute.
Make Department a derived attribute of COURSE only.
Create DEPARTMENT as a separate entity type and relate it to STUDENT, INSTRUCTOR, and COURSE.
Keep each Department attribute and copy its value into every related entity.
questions.explanation: An attribute repeated across entity types may be promoted to an independent entity type with appropriate relationships, reducing repetition and allowing further properties to be represented. (§3.7)

image.alt: A larger entity-relationship model diagram with several entities and relationships.

questions.prompt: For an entity’s participation in relationship R, what does the constraint (0, 1) state in min-max notation?
choices: Every entity participates in exactly one R instance.
The entity participates in at least one and in no more than one R instance.
The entity participates in zero or more R instances with no upper bound.
Zero or one R instances; participation may be partial.
questions.explanation: Min-max values give the lower and upper participation counts for each entity; a minimum of zero means partial participation, and a maximum of one limits its instances. (§3.7)

image.alt: Two entities related in crow's foot notation, with line-end symbols for optionality and multiplicity.

questions.prompt: What are the three parts of a UML class box?
choices: Class name, attributes, and operations
Entity set, relationship instances, and keys
Class name, relationship names, and database files
Attributes, value sets, and cardinality ratios
questions.explanation: A UML class box has a top compartment for the class name, a middle compartment for attributes, and a bottom compartment for operations (§3.8).

image.alt: UML class diagram notation showing class boxes and relationship lines.

questions.prompt: Assume ER min-max labels appear beside the entity type whose participation they constrain. In UML class diagrams, what do multiplicities 1 and * mean, respectively, and where are their labels placed?
choices: 1 means 1..* and * means 0..1; multiplicities replace association lines.
1 means exactly one; * means zero or more; labels sit opposite ER min-max ends.
1 means 0..1 and * means 1..*; multiplicities appear at the same ends as ER min-max labels.
1 means exactly one relationship type and * means many entity types; labels appear inside class boxes.
questions.explanation: In UML, 1 denotes exactly one and * denotes zero or more. UML multiplicity labels appear at the opposite association ends from ER min-max labels (§3.8).

image.alt: A UML class diagram association drawn as a line between two classes.

questions.prompt: A UML design models DEPENDENT objects whose names distinguish dependents belonging to the same EMPLOYEE. Which construct can represent the owner link and this discriminator?
choices: An operation listed below the EMPLOYEE attributes
An aggregation with no qualifier or partial key
A qualified association on EMPLOYEE uses a qualifier
A derived attribute on the DEPENDENT class
questions.explanation: A UML qualified association can represent the identifying relationship and place the partial key, called a discriminator, in a box attached to the owner class. (§3.8)

image.alt: A UML class diagram association drawn as a line between two classes.

questions.prompt: What is a ternary relationship type?
choices: A relationship type with three attributes and two entity types
A relationship type in which each entity participates three times
A set of three binary relationship types with identical meanings
A relationship type with three participating entity types
questions.explanation: Relationship degree counts participating entity types; degree three is called ternary. (§3.9)

image.alt: ER diagram in Chen notation with entity rectangles, attribute ovals and relationship diamonds.

questions.prompt: A database separately records that supplier S can supply part P, project J uses P, and S supplies some part to J. What can be concluded about a ternary SUPPLY instance (S, J, P)?
choices: No: pairwise facts do not entail the ternary tuple.
It exists only if each binary relationship has total participation.
It is equivalent to the three binary facts whenever the part has a unique name.
It must exist because all three pairwise relationships exist.
questions.explanation: The three binary relationships have different pairwise meanings and do not necessarily imply the specific supplier-project-part association represented by SUPPLY. (§3.9)

image.alt: ER diagram in Chen notation with entity rectangles, attribute ovals and relationship diamonds.

questions.prompt: In ternary SUPPLY(SUPPLIER, PROJECT, PART), a rule says that for each project-part pair, at most one supplier is used. Which combination identifies a SUPPLY instance under this rule?
choices: All three participating entities are always required
SUPPLIER and PROJECT
SUPPLIER and PART
PROJECT and PART
questions.explanation: A fixed PROJECT-PART pair determines a single SUPPLIER, so the (project, part) combination is a key for the relationship set. (§3.9)

image.alt: A sample entity relationship diagram showing entities, relationships and cardinalities.

questions.prompt: For a ternary relationship, what is the difference between a 1/M/N mark on a participation arc and a (min,max) constraint?
choices: The 1/M/N marks specify attribute domains, while (min,max) identifies weak entities.
1/M/N constrains which participant combination determines an instance; (min,max) gives participation bounds.
1/M/N gives participation bounds; (min,max) determines the relationship key.
Both notations specify exactly the same constraints and can always be substituted for one another.
questions.explanation: On n-ary relationships, cardinality marks can express key constraints; min-max values constrain how many relationship instances each entity participates in and do not determine the key. (§3.9)

image.alt: The same one-to-many relationship drawn in several ER notations side by side.

questions.prompt: For `COURSE_OFFERING` entities, assume `SecId` is unique across all offerings and every offering must have at least five students. Which statement correctly combines these rules?
choices: Course name is unique across offerings, and every offering has one student
Room number is unique across the university, and students can take only one offering
SecId is unique; every offering has at least five students
SecNo is unique across all years, and each offering must have exactly five students
questions.explanation: The stated rules require SecId to be unique across all course offerings and each offering to have at least five students (§3.10).

image.alt: A larger entity-relationship model diagram with several entities and relationships.

questions.prompt: A STUDENT has a composite `SName` attribute with separately addressable given, middle, and family name components. Which component list represents that attribute?
choices: First name, middle name, and last name
Student ID, major code, and birth date
Address, phone, and department name
Course name, course code, and course level
questions.explanation: SName is described as composed of FName, MName, and LName. (§3.10)

image.alt: An entity box shown together with one of its attributes in an ER diagram.

questions.prompt: A `COURSE_OFFERING` has `CourseCode`, `OfferNo`, `Term`, `Year`, `Room`, `DaysTimes`, and `InstructorId`. The design requires uniqueness for (OfferNo, Term, Year, CourseCode), (Term, Year, Room, DaysTimes), and (Term, Year, DaysTimes, InstructorId). Which combinations are unique? Select all that apply.
choices: Course level, credits, building, and student ID
Offering number, term, year, and course code
Term, year, classroom, and days/times
Term, year, days/times, and instructor ID
questions.explanation: The three combinations stated in the prompt are the required uniqueness constraints; the unrelated course, building, and student attributes are not among them (§3.10).

image.alt: A sample entity relationship diagram showing entities, relationships and cardinalities.

questions.prompt: A `COURSE_OFFERING` must have at least five students enrolled, with no specified upper limit. What min-max constraint represents an offering’s participation in TAKES?
choices: (0,N), allowing participation to start at zero
(1,1), requiring exactly one student per offering
(1,N), requiring at least one student per offering
questions.explanation: A minimum of five students and no fixed upper bound are represented as (5,N) for COURSE_OFFERING participation in TAKES (§3.10).

image.alt: Two entities related in crow's foot notation, with line-end symbols for optionality and multiplicity.
